problem:
Express the Maclaurin series expansion for $x\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ given by

$$
x\operatorname{sin}⁡x={x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{6}}{5!}-\frac{{x}^{8}}{7!}+⋯
$$

using sigma notation.

feedback.problem:
Express the Maclaurin series expansion for $\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}},$ given by

$$
\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}=1+2x+3{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3}+⋯\,,\,x\in (-1,1)
$$

using sigma notation.
feedback.worked_solution:
The first four terms of the series are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =1 \\ {a}_{1} & =2x \\ {a}_{2} & =3{x}^{2} \\ {a}_{3} & =4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we can express these terms using a common format, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & ={x}^{0} \\ {a}_{1} & =(1+1){x}^{1} \\ {a}_{2} & =(2+1){x}^{2} \\ {a}_{3} & =(3+1){x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We deduce that the general formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=(n+1){x}^{n}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(n+1){x}^{n}\,.
$$
